title: QUIC & HTTP/3
summary: HTTP/2 hit a wall with TCP. QUIC rebuilt transport from scratch over UDP — faster handshakes, independent streams, and connections that survive network switches.

blocks.markdown:
**QUIC** is a transport protocol built over UDP that replaces TCP for web traffic. **HTTP/3** is HTTP running on top of QUIC.

- Created by Google (2012), standardised by IETF in 2021 (RFC 9000).
- Solves TCP's three core pains: head-of-line blocking, slow handshakes, broken connections on network change.
- TLS 1.3 is baked in — all QUIC traffic is encrypted by default.
- See also: [tcp-deep-dive](tcp-deep-dive), [tls-ssl](tls-ssl), [http-https](http-https).

**Head-of-line (HoL) blocking**: TCP delivers bytes in order. If one packet is lost, TCP holds back all later packets until the gap is filled — even if they belong to completely unrelated requests.

- HTTP/2 multiplexed many requests over one TCP connection to avoid opening many sockets.
- But a single lost TCP segment stalls every stream at once — HoL blocking at the transport layer.
- This bottleneck is invisible to the application; TCP silently queues data behind the gap.

Opening a new HTTPS connection over TCP costs **3 round-trips** before the first byte of real data:

1. TCP 3-way handshake (1.5 RTT)
2. TLS handshake (1–2 RTT)

On a 50 ms RTT link that is 150–300 ms of pure setup — felt by every fresh connection.

**RTT (round-trip time)**: time for a packet to reach the server and a reply to return.

A TCP connection is identified by a 4-tuple: **{src IP, src port, dst IP, dst port}**. Change any element and TCP treats it as a different connection — the old one breaks.

- Switching from Wi-Fi to cellular changes your IP → the TCP connection dies.
- The app must reconnect and redo the full handshake, interrupting streaming or file transfers.

**UDP** is connectionless — it fires packets with no ordering or delivery guarantee. QUIC uses UDP as a thin carrier and **reimplements** everything TCP provides, plus more:

- Reliability and retransmission (per stream, not global)
- Congestion control
- Flow control
- Connection identity (not tied to IP)

Building on UDP lets QUIC live in user space and be updated without OS kernel changes — a key deployment advantage.

blocks.subTitle: 0-RTT and 1-RTT handshakes
blocks.markdown:
QUIC fuses the transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes into one.

- **1-RTT**: first connection to a server — crypto keys agreed in 1 round-trip, data flows immediately after.
- **0-RTT (zero round-trip time resumption)**: if client and server talked before, QUIC can send application data with the very first packet — no waiting at all.

**Trade-off**: 0-RTT data is vulnerable to replay attacks (an attacker re-sends the first packet). Only use it for idempotent requests.

QUIC's streams are **truly independent**: a lost packet only blocks the stream it belongs to.

<<< Image: two side-by-side diagrams on a dark background. Left panel labelled 'HTTP/2 over TCP — one byte stream': three coloured request bars (red, blue, green) stacked in a single pipe; a red X on the red bar causes blue and green to queue behind it with a 'stalled' label. Right panel labelled 'HTTP/3 over QUIC — independent streams': same three bars in separate lanes inside one QUIC connection box; red X on red lane has no effect on blue and green lanes, which flow freely. Arrow labels: left 'HoL blocking', right 'No HoL blocking'. >>>

- In TCP, all streams share one byte-sequence number space — any gap freezes all.
- In QUIC each stream has its own sequence space; the receiver delivers other streams while retransmitting only the lost packet.

QUIC identifies a connection with a **Connection ID** — a random token chosen by the client, not tied to any IP or port.

- When your IP changes (Wi-Fi → cellular), the Connection ID stays the same.
- The server recognises the same Connection ID in the new packets and keeps the connection alive.
- Result: video calls, large downloads, and long-lived sessions survive network switches without reconnecting.

**HTTP/3** is HTTP semantics (methods, headers, status codes) carried over QUIC instead of TCP.

- Replaces HTTP/2's binary framing layer with QUIC streams.
- Uses **QPACK** for header compression (replaces HPACK) — designed to avoid HoL blocking in header delivery.
- Negotiated via the **Alt-Svc** response header or HTTPS DNS records: server tells the browser "try QUIC next time."

HTTP/3 does not change how you write APIs — the semantics are identical to HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2.

blocks.subTitle: HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3 at a glance
blocks.markdown:
Key differences in the transport layer.

| Feature | HTTP/2 over TCP | HTTP/3 over QUIC |
|---|---|---|
| Transport | TCP | UDP + QUIC |
| HoL blocking | Yes (TCP level) | No (per-stream) |
| Handshake | 3+ RTT | 1-RTT / 0-RTT |
| Connection migration | No | Yes (Connection ID) |
| Encryption | TLS added on top | TLS 1.3 built in |

QUIC is fast but not a free lunch.

- **Middlebox interference**: firewalls and NATs often block or rate-limit UDP. QUIC falls back to TCP+TLS automatically.
- **CPU overhead**: encryption is per-packet; QUIC uses more CPU than plaintext TCP, though hardware offload is improving.
- **Ossification risk solved**: because QUIC is mostly opaque to middleboxes (all encrypted), the network can't inspect or modify it — which is both a security win and a debugging challenge.
- **Adoption**: Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Cloudflare, Google, Meta — all support HTTP/3. ~30% of web traffic as of 2024.

blocks.subTitle: Why QUIC was created
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Why was QUIC created if HTTP/2 already multiplexed streams?**

HTTP/2 multiplexing fixes application-level HoL blocking, but the fix lives above TCP. TCP still delivers bytes in order across the whole connection — one lost segment blocks every stream. QUIC owns the transport layer and makes streams truly independent, plus collapses the handshake and adds connection migration.

blocks.subTitle: Why UDP and not a new TCP option
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Why does QUIC run over UDP instead of extending TCP?**

TCP is implemented in OS kernels. Deploying a new TCP option takes years — ISPs, middleboxes, and OS vendors all need to update. UDP packets are passed straight to user space; QUIC can iterate quickly and ship as a library update. The trade-off is that QUIC must reimplement everything TCP gave for free (reliability, congestion control).

**Q: What is connection migration in QUIC?**

QUIC tags connections with a Connection ID rather than the 4-tuple (IP+port). When your IP changes, the server recognises the same ID and continues the session — no reconnect needed.
